explanation: The public band descriptors require a clear overview of main trends, differences or stages for Band 7 in Task Achievement. The overview is a short summary of the whole picture — specific figures belong in the body paragraphs, and personal opinions never belong in Task 1.
hint: Think summary, not details — and never numbers.
options: A detailed description of every data point in the chart
A 1–2 sentence summary of the main trends or features, with no specific figures
Your personal opinion about what the data means
A conclusion recommending what should be done
source: IELTS Academic Writing Task 1 public band descriptors — Task Achievement (ielts.org); IDP IELTS official overview guide (ielts.idp.com)
stem: What is an overview in IELTS Academic Writing Task 1?

explanation: Option C summarises the main trend with no figures — a proper overview. A dumps data mechanically (Band 5 behaviour), D gives an opinion (never in Task 1), and B is too vague to show understanding.
hint: The examiner wants the whole picture in one or two sentences.
options: In January it was 5°C, in February 6°C, in March 9°C, and so on through the year.
The graph shows information about temperature.
Overall, temperatures rose steadily from winter lows to a summer peak before falling again towards December.
I think this city is far too cold in winter.
source: IELTS Academic Writing Task 1 public band descriptors — Task Achievement (ielts.org); IDP IELTS official overview guide (ielts.idp.com)
stem: A line graph shows a city's average monthly temperature: low in winter, peaking in July, falling afterwards. Which is the best overview sentence?

explanation: Official preparation guidance notes the overview may go at the end, but placing it right after the introduction is safest — under time pressure it is the paragraph most often forgotten, and without a clear overview Task Achievement cannot pass Band 5.
hint: Put the most-marked paragraph where you cannot forget it.
options: Right after the introduction, before the detail paragraphs
Only as the very first sentence of the whole report
Hidden in the middle of a body paragraph
Task 1 does not need an overview at all
source: IDP IELTS official overview guide — 'Importance of an overview in Academic Writing Task 1' (ielts.idp.com); IELTS Task 1 public band descriptors, Task Achievement
stem: Where is the safest place to put the overview paragraph?

explanation: An overview never contains specific data — figures like 20,000 and 45,000 belong in the body paragraphs. An overview with numbers is a detail paragraph, not a summary.
hint: If it has a number in it, it does not belong in the overview.
options: Overall, sales increased over the period.
Sales rose from 20,000 units in 2010 to 45,000 units in 2020.
The most noticeable feature was the sharp rise after 2015.
In contrast, profits remained broadly stable throughout.
source: IDP IELTS official overview guide — overviews summarise trends with no data/numbers (ielts.idp.com); IELTS Task 1 public band descriptors
stem: Which sentence must NOT appear in an overview paragraph?

explanation: This captures the key comparison — highest versus lowest — with no figures, which is exactly what an overview does. Listing every figure is mechanical detail-dumping; vague comments add nothing.
hint: Highest versus lowest — that is the story of this chart.
options: Country A sold 100,000 cars, Country B sold 150,000, Country C sold 120,000 and Country D sold 90,000.
Cars are clearly important in all four countries.
Overall, Country B recorded the highest sales while Country D recorded the lowest.
The chart gives information about car sales in four countries.
source: IELTS Academic Writing Task 1 public band descriptors — Task Achievement: overview of main trends/differences (ielts.org)
stem: A bar chart shows car sales (in thousands): Country A 100, B 150, C 120, D 90. Which is the best overview sentence?

explanation: The Band 5 descriptor for Task Achievement describes exactly this: detail recounted mechanically with no clear overview. No overview caps the score however good the grammar is.
hint: Check what Band 5 says about overviews.
options: It can still reach Band 8 if the grammar is excellent.
It is limited to around Band 5: detail is recounted mechanically with no clear overview.
Only Coherence and Cohesion is affected, not Task Achievement.
The overview only matters in Task 2, not Task 1.
source: IELTS Writing Task 1 public band descriptors (public version) — Task Achievement bands 5–7 (British Council / IDP / Cambridge English)
stem: A response describes every data point accurately but has no clear overview. What do the band descriptors say about Task Achievement?

explanation: For process diagrams the overview summarises the main stages without step-by-step detail. One detail, an irrelevant comment, or empty sequencing words all fail the overview's job.
hint: Stages, not steps — summarise the whole process.
options: Overall, the process consists of four main stages, from picking the beans to brewing the coffee.
The beans are picked by hand from the coffee plants.
Coffee is one of the most popular drinks in the world.
First one thing happens, then another thing, then another.
source: IELTS Academic Writing Task 1 format — process diagrams assessed on overview of stages (ielts.org); IELTS Liz Task 1 structure guidance (ieltsliz.com)
stem: A process diagram shows how coffee is made: picking → roasting → grinding → brewing. Which is the best overview?

explanation: The official IELTS format requires a minimum of 150 words for Task 1 (and 250 for Task 2). Responses below the minimum are penalised.
hint: Task 2 needs 250 — Task 1 needs fewer.
options: 100 words
200 words
250 words
150 words
source: IELTS Academic Writing test format — ielts.org (British Council / IDP / Cambridge English)
stem: What is the minimum word count for Writing Task 1?

explanation: IELTS recommends about 20 minutes on Task 1 and 40 minutes on Task 2, reflecting that Task 2 carries twice the weight in the Writing score.
hint: Task 2 is worth double, so it gets double the time.
options: 10 minutes
30 minutes
40 minutes
20 minutes
source: IELTS Academic Writing test format — ielts.org (British Council / IDP / Cambridge English)
stem: How much time should you spend on Writing Task 1?

explanation: Task 2 contributes twice as much as Task 1 to the Writing band score, so Task 1 counts for one third. This is why time management favours Task 2.
hint: Task 2 counts double.
options: Half of the Writing score
Two thirds of the Writing score
It is not scored separately
One third of the Writing score
source: IELTS Academic Writing test format — task weighting (ielts.org)
stem: What share of the Writing score comes from Task 1?

explanation: A continuous upward movement is a steady rise. Fluctuate means moving up and down; stable means little or no change; a sharp fall is the opposite direction.
hint: One direction, no wobbles.
options: Fluctuating
Rising steadily
Falling sharply
Remaining stable
source: IELTS Academic Writing Task 1 — trend vocabulary for line graphs; IELTS Liz line graph vocabulary guidance (ieltsliz.com)
stem: A line graph shows smartphone users climbing from 1 billion (2015) to 3 billion (2025) without interruption. How is this trend best described?

explanation: Plummeted describes a sudden, steep fall — exactly a drop from 500 to 100. Soared is a steep rise; edged up is a tiny rise; levelled off means flattening after change.
hint: 500 down to 100 is not a gentle change.
options: Soared
Edged up
Levelled off
Plummeted
source: IELTS Academic Writing Task 1 — trend vocabulary: verbs of change and degree (ielts.org preparation materials)
stem: 'Sales dropped from 500 to 100 in a single year.' Which verb fits best?

explanation: Tiny movements around 8% mean the figure was broadly stable. Words like dramatically and wildly overstate the change — examiners reward accurate degree language under Lexical Resource.
hint: 8.0 to 8.1 is not dramatic.
options: Rose dramatically
Fell steadily
Remained relatively stable
Fluctuated wildly
source: IELTS Academic Writing Task 1 — describing degree of change; public band descriptors, Lexical Resource (ielts.org)
stem: Unemployment stood at 8.0%, 8.1%, 7.9% and 8.0% over four years. Which description is most accurate?

explanation: Soared and surged both mean a sharp rise. The other pairs mix a rise with a fall, or are both falls — mixing them up is a common beginner error that costs marks.
hint: Both words must point upward.
options: Rose / declined
Soared / surged
Dipped / dropped
Fell / plunged
source: IELTS Academic Writing Task 1 — trend vocabulary (ielts.org preparation materials)
stem: Which pair of verbs both describe an increase?

explanation: Fluctuate means to rise and fall irregularly — the key word for unstable, wavy data on a line graph.
hint: Think of a wavy line.
options: It moved up and down repeatedly
It stayed exactly the same
It increased slowly every year
It stopped changing completely
source: IELTS Academic Writing Task 1 — trend vocabulary (ielts.org preparation materials)
stem: 'The figure fluctuated throughout the decade.' What does this mean?

explanation: This captures both phases with accurate degree language — gradually versus sharply. Describing phases correctly is the core skill Task 1 trends questions reward.
hint: Two phases — describe both.
options: Exports fell throughout the period.
Exports grew gradually before rising sharply after 2015.
Exports remained unchanged for the whole period.
Exports moved randomly with no clear pattern.
source: IELTS Academic Writing Task 1 — describing trends in phases (ielts.org preparation materials)
stem: A line graph shows exports climbing slowly from 2010 to 2015, then shooting upward from 2015 to 2020. Which summary is best?

explanation: Rocketed signals a very steep, dramatic rise. Edged up, inched up and grew slightly all describe small increases — choosing the right degree of change matters for Lexical Resource.
hint: Which one sounds fastest?
options: Edged up
Inched up
Rocketed
Grew slightly
source: IELTS Academic Writing Task 1 — verbs of change and adverbs of degree; public band descriptors, Lexical Resource (ielts.org)
stem: Which verb shows the strongest increase?

explanation: Line graphs are designed to show movement over time. Pie charts show shares at a single point; maps show layout; process diagrams show stages of a process.
hint: Time runs along the bottom axis.
options: A pie chart
A map of a single city
A line graph
A process diagram
source: IELTS Academic Writing Task 1 — visual types and what they show (ielts.org)
stem: Which type of visual is best for showing change over time?

explanation: A peak is the highest point on a graph — the opposite of a trough or lowest point.
hint: Think of a mountain top.
options: It reached its lowest point
It stayed at the same level
It reached its highest point
It dropped to zero
source: IELTS Academic Writing Task 1 — trend vocabulary (ielts.org preparation materials)
stem: 'Production peaked at 900 units in June.' What does 'peaked' mean here?

explanation: The crossover is the noticeable feature an overview should capture. Colours and page layout are never key features — the examiner marks what you say about the data.
hint: What would you tell a friend about this graph?
options: Both lines are drawn in blue ink.
The graph covers a period of ten years.
The two lines crossed in 2018, reversing their positions.
2018 falls in the middle of the horizontal axis.
source: IELTS Academic Writing Task 1 public band descriptors — Task Achievement: presenting key features (ielts.org)
stem: Two lines on a graph: one rises, one falls, and they cross in 2018. What is the key feature?

explanation: Comparing the extremes — largest versus smallest — is the key feature. One isolated figure is just a detail; vague comments and describing the chart's appearance add nothing.
hint: Biggest versus smallest.
options: Delhi had the largest population while Tokyo had the smallest.
Tokyo's population was 14 million.
All four cities are extremely crowded places.
The chart uses vertical bars of different heights.
source: IELTS Academic Writing Task 1 public band descriptors — Task Achievement: clearly presents and highlights key features (ielts.org)
stem: A bar chart shows city populations: Tokyo 14m, Delhi 32m, Shanghai 28m, São Paulo 22m. Which is the best key-feature sentence?

explanation: Grouping and comparing is the skill Band 7 requires — 'clearly presents and highlights key features'. Listing every figure is the mechanical approach capped at Band 5.
hint: Group, don't list.
options: A was 10, B was 20, C was 30 and D was 40.
B and D together accounted for most of the total, far exceeding A and C.
The data shown here is very interesting indeed.
There are four separate categories in the chart.
source: IELTS Writing Task 1 public band descriptors (public version) — Task Achievement bands 5–7 (British Council / IDP / Cambridge English)
stem: Which sentence selects key features instead of listing everything?

explanation: This summarises the pattern across all countries with no figures — a proper overview. One detail, an opinion, or stating the obvious all miss the overview's job.
hint: What happened everywhere — and where most?
options: Every country improved, with the largest gains in the countries that started lowest.
Country X stood at 62% in 1990.
Literacy is clearly important for economic development.
The table presents data for two different years.
source: IELTS Academic Writing Task 1 public band descriptors — Task Achievement: clear overview of main trends/differences (ielts.org)
stem: A table shows literacy rates in 1990 versus 2020 for five countries: all rose, with the fastest rises in the two lowest-ranked countries. Which is the best overview line?

explanation: Task 1 is a factual report on the visual — personal views belong in Task 2 essays. Examiners penalise opinions in Task 1 under Task Achievement.
hint: Task 1 reports; Task 2 argues.
options: Give your personal opinion about the data
Compare the main features of the data
Write a clear overview paragraph
Support your descriptions with selected figures
source: IELTS Academic Writing Task 1 format — report, not essay (ielts.org); IELTS Liz Task 1 guidance (ieltsliz.com)
stem: What should you NEVER do in Academic Writing Task 1?

explanation: It contrasts two trends in a single sentence — the comparison skill Task 1 rewards. Note Task 1 has no conclusion paragraph and no opinions, so those options are traps.
hint: Two fuels, opposite directions, one sentence.
options: A mechanical list of numbers
A personal opinion about energy
A clear comparison of two key features
A concluding paragraph
source: IELTS Academic Writing Task 1 — comparing data; IELTS Liz Task 1 structure guidance (ieltsliz.com)
stem: 'While coal declined steadily, gas rose to become the largest source.' This sentence is an example of:

explanation: Examiners warn against describing every detail — selecting key features is what is actually marked. Month-by-month data-dumping across ten years is the classic error that caps Task Achievement.
hint: More detail is not more marks.
options: The overall trend across the decade
The wettest and the driest years
The exact rainfall for every single month of all ten years
One year in which rainfall changed sharply
source: IELTS Academic Writing Task 1 public band descriptors — Task Achievement: selecting key features vs mechanical detail (ielts.org)
stem: You have ten years of monthly rainfall data. Which detail matters LEAST for your report?

explanation: For maps, 'trends' become 'main changes or developments' — the overview must capture the biggest ones. Opinions and empty statements score nothing.
hint: What changed most?
options: The maps show a town in two different years.
I personally prefer the new road layout.
1990 was a very long time ago.
The most significant changes were the replacement of farmland with housing and the construction of a new road.
source: IELTS Academic Writing Task 1 — map tasks: describing main changes (ielts.org); IELTS Liz map vocabulary guidance (ieltsliz.com)
stem: Two maps show a town in 1990 and 2020: farmland has been replaced by housing and a new road has been built. Which best states the key features?

explanation: Key features are defined as the most significant similarities and differences — this is what the Band 7+ descriptor asks candidates to present and highlight clearly.
hint: Significant, not random.
options: Random pairs of numbers from the chart
Your own life experiences
A different chart you remember well
The most significant similarities and differences in the data
source: IELTS Writing Task 1 public band descriptors (public version) — Task Achievement: 'clearly presents and highlights key features' (British Council / IDP / Cambridge English)
stem: In Task 1, your comparisons should focus on:

explanation: This groups the joint leaders and compares them against the lowest, with data support — the key-feature skill. Listing all four figures is mechanical; the other options say nothing about the data.
hint: Joint top versus bottom.
options: Bananas and oranges were the most popular at 45kg each, more than double the figure for grapes.
Apples were 30kg, bananas 45kg, oranges 45kg and grapes 20kg.
Fruit is healthy and everyone should eat more of it.
There are four different types of fruit in the chart.
source: IELTS Academic Writing Task 1 public band descriptors — Task Achievement: selecting and comparing key features (ielts.org)
stem: A bar chart shows fruit eaten (kg): apples 30, bananas 45, oranges 45, grapes 20. Which is the best key-feature sentence?

explanation: These four criteria appear in the official band descriptors for Writing. The last option describes the Speaking test — mixing up the two tests' criteria is a common beginner mistake.
hint: The last option is the Speaking test.
options: Task Achievement, Coherence and Cohesion, Lexical Resource, Grammatical Range and Accuracy
Spelling, Handwriting, Length and Speed
Ideas, Opinions, Stories and Conclusions
Vocabulary, Grammar, Pronunciation and Fluency
source: IELTS Writing band descriptors (public version) — four assessment criteria (British Council / IDP / Cambridge English)
